qt: to the Commission Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

The Commission is considering drastically cutting funding for the promotion of European food under the ‘Enjoy, it’s from Europe’ scheme, including a reduction in funding for the MULTI campaign from EUR 60 million to EUR 20 million. At the same time, despite opposition from some Member States, including Poland, the Commission is consistently opening up the EU market to ever-increasing imports of agri-food products from Ukraine and Mercosur countries. European farmers are forced to comply with some of the most stringent and costly production standards in the world, while cheaper products manufactured without a comparable system of requirements, controls and traceability are entering the EU market. In the case of imports from Ukraine, serious concerns regarding the quality and testing of certain products, as well as market destabilisation, have been raised repeatedly by Member States and farmers. In light of the above: 1.
Why is the Commission cutting funding for the promotion of European food while increasing access to the EU market for cheaper products from third countries?

Why is the Commission ignoring the objections of some Member States and concerns regarding the quality and testing of imported food rather than protecting producers who meet the EU’s stringent standards?

Is the Commission’s policy intended to create a situation in which European farmers bear the costs of EU regulations while their place in the market is taken by cheaper food produced to lower standards?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.11.2026) As the Commission set out in its reply to Written Question P-002789/2026, ‘the allocation for 2027 remains subject to possible adjustments to be proposed in the Amending Letter to the Draft EU Budget 2027’. Similarly to previous years, the Commission managed to propose a significant reinforcement of EUR 50 million for the multi-programmes promotion actions under direct management. This increase reflects the importance of promotion activities for the agricultural sector. In addition, the Commission has allocated EUR 35 million in the 2026 budget for a new EU-wide campaign on European food, to be rolled out in 2027 across all 27 Member States. The EU applies the same robust health and safety standards for products imported into the EU as it does for those produced in the EU. When negotiating trade agreements with other countries or regions, the EU does not compromise on these standards. Food products imported from third countries, regardless of their origin, must comply with EU food safety import requirements. They are enforced through rigorous controls and audits, which have been recently reinforced1. Under the Vision for Agriculture and Food2 the Commission pursues, in line with international rules3, a stronger alignment of production standards applied to imported products, notably as regards pesticides and animal welfare. In that respect, the Commission is working to avoid that the most hazardous pesticides banned in the EU for health and environmental reasons would be imported back into the EU through imported products. In the area of animal welfare, the Commission will pursue that future legislative proposals apply the same standards for products produced in the EU and those imported from third countries, in a way that is compliant with the World Trade Organization (WTO) rules and based on an impact assessment.
